document_title: ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow: Hypertension in Adults

sections.heading: Diagnosis and staging of hypertension
sections.content: Diagnosis is based on the average of two or more readings on two or more occasions. Stage 1 is 140-159/90-99 mmHg and Stage 2 is >=160/100 mmHg. Assess for target-organ damage and cardiovascular risk before starting therapy. Where feasible, confirm with out-of-office measurement.

sections.heading: Pharmacological management of hypertension
sections.content: First-line options include a calcium-channel blocker (e.g. amlodipine), an ACE inhibitor or ARB (e.g. enalapril/telmisartan), or a thiazide-like diuretic. In adults under 55, an ACE inhibitor/ARB is often preferred; a CCB or thiazide is reasonable in older adults. Combination therapy is appropriate when a single agent does not achieve the target. Review adherence and lifestyle measures (salt reduction, weight, activity) at every visit.

sections.heading: Red flags and referral
sections.content: Consider urgent referral for accelerated hypertension (>=180/120 with target-organ damage), suspected secondary hypertension in the young, or resistant hypertension on three agents including a diuretic.

document_title: ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus

sections.heading: Diagnosis of type 2 diabetes
sections.content: Diagnosis is supported by fasting plasma glucose >=126 mg/dL, 2-hour post-load glucose >=200 mg/dL, HbA1c >=6.5%, or a random glucose >=200 mg/dL with classic symptoms. Confirm with a repeat test unless the patient is symptomatic with unequivocal hyperglycaemia.

sections.heading: Glycaemic management of type 2 diabetes
sections.content: Metformin is the preferred first-line pharmacotherapy alongside lifestyle modification, unless contraindicated (e.g. eGFR below 30). When glycaemic targets are not met, guidelines support adding a second agent such as a sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitor, or SGLT2 inhibitor, individualised to comorbidity and cost. Reassess HbA1c every 3 months until stable.

sections.heading: Screening for complications
sections.content: Screen at least annually for retinopathy, nephropathy (urine albumin and eGFR), and diabetic foot. Blood-pressure and lipid control substantially reduce cardiovascular risk in diabetes.

document_title: ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow: Community-Acquired Pneumonia

sections.heading: Assessment and severity of community-acquired pneumonia
sections.content: Assess severity with CRB-65 (confusion, respiratory rate >=30, BP <90/60, age >=65). Pulse oximetry guides oxygen need. Low-severity disease can often be managed in the community; higher scores support hospital assessment.

sections.heading: Antibiotic management of community-acquired pneumonia
sections.content: For low-severity community-acquired pneumonia, guidelines support oral amoxicillin as first-line, with a macrolide (e.g. azithromycin) or doxycycline as an alternative in penicillin allergy. Reassess at 48-72 hours. Higher-severity disease warrants combination therapy and consideration of inpatient care.

document_title: ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow: Dengue Fever

sections.heading: Warning signs and monitoring in dengue
sections.content: Warning signs include abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, and a rising haematocrit with a rapid platelet fall. Monitor haematocrit and platelets during the critical (plasma-leak) phase around defervescence.

sections.heading: Fluid management in dengue
sections.content: Management is largely supportive with careful isotonic fluid therapy titrated to the plasma-leak phase. Paracetamol is preferred for fever; NSAIDs and aspirin are best avoided because of bleeding risk. Admit patients with warning signs or significant comorbidity.

document_title: ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow: Acute Coronary Syndrome

sections.heading: Recognition of acute coronary syndrome
sections.content: Suspected ACS warrants an immediate 12-lead ECG and troponin where available. Atypical presentations are common in diabetics, women, and the elderly. Time-critical recognition and transfer underpin outcomes.

sections.heading: Initial management of acute coronary syndrome
sections.content: Initial measures supported by guidelines include aspirin (unless contraindicated), pain relief, and urgent referral to a facility capable of reperfusion. Do not delay transfer for investigations in a clearly evolving event.

document_title: WHO Guidelines: Management of Uncomplicated Malaria

sections.heading: Diagnosis of malaria
sections.content: Parasitological confirmation by microscopy or a rapid diagnostic test is recommended before treatment wherever possible. Species and parasite density guide therapy and severity assessment.

sections.heading: Treatment of uncomplicated malaria
sections.content: Artemisinin-based combination therapy is the recommended treatment for uncomplicated falciparum malaria, with regimens following national programme guidance. Severe malaria requires parenteral therapy and referral.

document_title: NICE Guideline: Acute Gastroenteritis in Adults

sections.heading: Management of acute gastroenteritis
sections.content: Most acute gastroenteritis is self-limiting; oral rehydration and continued feeding are the mainstay. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated. Assess for dehydration and red flags (bloody stool, high fever, severe abdominal pain) that warrant further evaluation.
